prize_parts.citation: for the development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is a defined discovery with a clear mechanistic basis: ligand design (bulky biaryl and hindered alkyl phosphines, and Hartwig's mechanistic work on oxidative addition, amide binding and reductive elimination) turned a narrow reaction into a general one. It is used daily in pharmaceutical, agrochemical and organic-materials synthesis, has three decades of independent confirmation, and is the most stable of the shortlisted cases in attribution, since two people independently built the general method. Four other members already rank it in their top five, so it is the only candidate with broad cross-subfield support and a clean two-laureate citation.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that it can be read as a sequel to the 2010 cross-coupling prize, which could dilute its perceived novelty, and that the Kosugi tin-amide precedent complicates priority. I also acknowledge that my ranking reflects a preference for enabling methods and that I rely on recollection for the 1994-1995 timeline. Against this, the C-N bond was not covered in 2010, and Kosugi's reaction was not general or ligand-controlled.

responses.point: C-N coupling turned aryl amine synthesis from a harsh, narrow problem into a routine operation, but the committee may view it as an extension of the 2010 prize and the 1994-1995 priority exchange is hard to verify.
responses.response: I agree with the merit case and with the two-person configuration. On the 2010 worry, I think a distinct bond type, a distinct ligand-control principle and a distinct mechanistic problem (C-N reductive elimination from a Pd amide) make this a separate achievement and not a repeat. On priority I side with you that Kosugi is a precedent, but a tin-amide reaction of limited scope is not the general method; I would not add his name, though the citation wording should not claim the first-ever reaction.

responses.point: Hartwig also appears in a separate C-H functionalization entry, so credit boundaries need care, and Kosugi and Migita-type precursors may weigh against the Buchwald/Hartwig generalization.
responses.response: A fair point on the boundaries, and the citation should be limited to C-N cross-coupling so that nothing from C-H functionalization is implied. I do not think the precursors outweigh the generalization: the contribution that changed practice was the ligand families and the mechanistic understanding, which both laureates supplied independently. I would resist widening the prize to three names for the sake of completeness.

responses.point: Phase separation (B002) is a physical-chemical idea of unusual generality with textbook-level maturity, and Hyman with Brangwynne is the cleanest pair, though omitting Rosen is a credit question.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual reach, but I am less persuaded on structural evidence: many in-cell claims of liquid phase behaviour still rest on overexpression and imaging, as Chabes also notes, and the discovery sits uneasily between chemistry and cell biology. B052 has no comparable doubt about whether the phenomenon is real or general. I would, however, accept B002 as a serious competitor if the committee wants a physical-chemistry prize, and I see its credit problem (Rosen, Pappu, Mittag) as larger than yours suggests.

responses.point: Base editing (B004) is a clean chemical-mechanism story on a single base with direct therapeutic reach, with Liu, Komor and Gaudelli as a fair configuration, but Kondo and Nishida's independent claim and overlap with CRISPR remain open.
responses.response: The deaminase chemistry and the directed evolution of an adenine deaminase acting on DNA are genuinely novel, and I rank B004 as a respectable alternative. My reservations are timing and credit: the 2020 CRISPR prize makes this look like a sequel, clinical evidence is still emerging, and the Target-AID priority question would make a three-person citation contentious. B052 carries none of these risks, so I would put it ahead.

responses.point: Long-range electron transfer through proteins (B009) is a quantitative physical mechanism underlying respiration and photosynthesis, overdue after four decades, with Gray and Winkler as a clean pair.
responses.response: I agree that the science is solid and that the Gray and Winkler work is mature. My concern is the one you list yourself: much of the framework traces to Marcus theory, already honoured, and to Dutton and Moser, who are outside the credited names. As a structural chemist I also want to see how much of the story rests on defined structures of engineered proteins. I do not see a path to majority support, but I would hear the case for it in round 2.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues who ranked B052 outside the top three regard it as too close to the 2010 prize.
How the committee will treat the Kosugi precedent in the citation wording.
Whether a majority will converge on B052 or split across B002, B004 and B037 as an alternative to a chemistry-centred prize.
Whether a two-part prize pairing C-N coupling with a materials or biological achievement would be preferable to a single part.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. None of the candidates are from Stockholm University or my own electron-crystallography field, and I have no known personal tie to Buchwald, Hartwig or Kosugi.
